title: Building a cozy dark-fantasy merge game solo with AI: what worked and what didn't [Pre-Alpha, Android]
author: luks83
selftext:
I'm a solo dev building Wicky: The Kind Dark, a quiet dark-fantasy merge-and-dice-road game with light settlement building, in Unity. Without AI I couldn't have started it, so I wanted to share how I'm using it and where it falls short.

**What AI does in the project:**

Code: I build the game in Unity (C#) with Claude Code as my main coding assistant. It writes and refactors most systems (merge board, road, seasons, save data, UI) and the build and capture tools. I set the design and review every change by playing builds on my phone. Claude also reads my playtest logs to flag pacing and economy problems, and I decide what changes.

Design and lore: The design, the story and the characters are mine. I use Claude for naming passes, for wording in-game text and for checking new drafts against my story bible and the game's actual rules, e.g. lining up an outside writer's draft with how the game works. Every decision is mine.

Art: The art in the build is placeholder, some of it AI-assisted. I make the 2D art with image models through Scenario (GPT Image, with my own reference portraits) and ChatGPT. Building and character art is painted over simple 3D block models rendered from the game camera, so the angle and scale stay right. 3D accessories come from my own front/side/back concept sheets through Rodin and Tripo, then get cleaned up in Blender. All art is colour-graded and checked at in-game size by hand. Final art will be reworked.

Marketing: Videos are mostly real gameplay, captured in-engine or recorded on my phone, with the game's own sound effects. Claude Code handles the editing (cuts, sound sync, captions) under my direction. A few short opening and closing shots are AI video (Minimax) made from my key art, and they're kept separate from the gameplay footage. Captions and post copy are drafted with Claude, and I edit them.

  
**What worked:**  
  
\- Video editing. Claude cut real gameplay together, synced the game's own sound effects to the exact frames and put the captions on the game's UI frame. The first trailer came out better than the editing services I'd looked at.

\- Item art. Running every generated item through the same colour-grading script made it pop off the board and look like one set.

  
**What didn't:**

\- Board tiles. They looked fine at full size but failed twice at cell size: one pattern read as a grid inside the grid, another as a symbol on every cell. Now I judge every asset at its real on-screen size.

\- Freehand building and character art never matched the camera angle or the size of the people. It only worked once I painted over 3D block models rendered from the game camera.

\- AI video wasted credits on anatomy errors: an extra arm, then a backwards hand. Now I check the start frame before every paid run.

\- 3D gear. The first export tore every seam open, and a backpack Claude said fit was floating off the character's back when seen from the side. I caught it, and fit checks are now zoomed shots from every angle.



**What I do by hand:**

Game feel, balance, final naming, and every decision about what stays in the game.

The game is in Pre-Alpha, so it's rough. If you want to look at how the result holds up, there's an Android sign-up here playwicky.com. I'd also like to hear how you handle consistency and review when AI is writing a lot of your code or assets.
